details:
**Utilitarianism**
The ethical theory that Bentham founded, later developed by John Stuart Mill. It holds that the right action is the one that produces the greatest overall happiness, measured as pleasure minus pain. Bentham's version, which judges each individual action by its consequences, is now often classed as act utilitarianism.

**Panopticon**
Bentham's design for a prison (also proposed for factories, schools, and hospitals) in which a central watchtower lets a single guard observe all the inmates, who cannot tell whether they are being watched at any moment. Michel Foucault made it a central image of modern surveillance and discipline in Discipline and Punish.

**Felicific calculus**
Bentham's method, also called the hedonic calculus, for measuring the amount of pleasure and pain an action will cause by adding and subtracting them. It weighs factors including intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (nearness), fecundity, purity, and extent (the number of people affected).

**An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation**
Bentham's most famous work, printed in 1780 and published in 1789. It sets out the principle of utility and the felicific calculus and applies them to law and punishment. It opens by declaring that "Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure."

**"The greatest happiness of the greatest number"**
The slogan summarizing Bentham's "greatest happiness principle," which he described as the measure of right and wrong and the foundation of morals and legislation.

**Auto-icon**
After Bentham's death in 1832, his body was dissected for science as he had requested, and his skeleton was padded, dressed in his own clothes, and topped with a wax head to form what he called an "auto-icon." It is displayed at University College London, and it is said to be brought to some meetings of the college council.

**"Nonsense upon stilts"**
Bentham's mocking description of natural and inalienable rights, which he considered meaningless fictions. The phrase comes from his attack on the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, known as Anarchical Fallacies.

**William Blackstone and A Fragment on Government**
Bentham's 1776 A Fragment on Government attacked the English jurist William Blackstone, whose Commentaries on the Laws of England praised the existing common law. It grew out of Bentham's longer critique of Blackstone, A Comment on the Commentaries.

**"Offences Against One's Self"**
Bentham's essay, written around 1785 but unpublished in his lifetime, arguing that homosexual acts cause no harm to others and should therefore not be punished. It is one of the earliest known arguments in English for decriminalizing homosexuality.

**Pannomion**
Bentham's term for his goal of a complete, codified body of law based on the principle of utility. He offered to draft such codes for several countries.

**Four sanctions**
Bentham identified four sources of the pleasures and pains that motivate behavior: the physical, political, moral, and religious sanctions. He later added the sanction of sympathy.

**Philip Beauchamp**
The pseudonym under which Bentham's controversial critique of religion, Analysis of the Influence of Natural Religion on the Temporal Happiness of Mankind (1822), was published. The work argued that religion does more harm than good to human happiness.

**"Emancipate Your Colonies!"**
Bentham's 1793 pamphlet addressed to the National Convention of revolutionary France, urging the French to give up their colonies.

**Defence of Usury**
Bentham's 1787 work arguing against legal limits on the interest rates that lenders may charge. It criticized Adam Smith's support for such limits.
